To the Editor of The Tribune.


Sir: As many college graduates will join woman's club societies, and those for social reform to be popular just now, a few comments on such may be suitable to show that no department of woman's work requires more severe study. Heretofore woman has chiefly restricted her moral teachings to the home, and her pupils have had heredity, for the most part, resembling her own, and environment she could in great measure create or control.


In the wider sphere which she enters, in undertaking to be "a public moral teacher," both the heredity and environment of her pupils are almost unknown quantities. She must therefore be well prepared by much study and thought to attempt to better the social body, otherwise more evil than good may result from her work. It is not sufficient that her motives be good. All religious persecutions have claimed good motives. She must be willing to study life in as many varied forms as possible and be able to make intelligent decisions. When investigation is made it will be discovered that the aim of the wisest and best men of the impotency of human effort to go on by the universal testimony of the race is that in a chaos of mass. Hence Jesus Christ appeared. The lesson this suggests is that social reform clubs should search the records of this greatest of social reformers, and practically con-


When the Israelites followed the teachings of Moses, the greatest moral teacher of antiquity, they rose to the highest elevation of sentiment; We have a greater than Moses to teach us, and have but to obey to reach a plane of social progress of which prophets could not dream of which the Spirit of God is being poured out on all men and both sons and daughters are witness-bearers of truth.


Let social reform clubs, then, study well the fundamental principles of their practice, as set forth in the Bible. Should such a course of study be adopted, the discovery will be made that what passes for Christianity in many cases is as far removed from the teachings of Christ as modern Buddhism and Confucianism is remote from the teachings of their founders; and club making such researches could show that while Christ's doctrines inculcate faith in God and man and are perfectly altruistic, modern Christianity, as illustrated by nine-tenths of its adherents, is just the opposite.


The studies to prepare women to be efficient social reformers are innumerable, but when ignorant women appear before the public as social reformers, no amount of stage manner or blatant parade of carefully memorized extracts from educational books or magazines will hasten the day of social reform. The country is flooded with such platform speakers who by effrontery and fraud are bringing into disrepute the real work of earnest scholars. Societies should guard against encouraging such, and only really cultured women should be allowed to speak before women's clubs.


Truly yours, etc., A. H.


University of Geneva, Aug. 1, 1895.

Since the annexation of Hawaii there has been a great demand for statistics relating to the trade of the country. The bureau of statistics at Washington has pub lished a special report on the sub ject which is very interesting.

 Hawaii imports everything ex- cept sugar, coffee and fruits. Sugar production, of course, is principal industry of the island, and what is not consumed there IS exported to the United States, which Ill 1896 took 99.64 per cent of the total exports of the islands and supplied 70.27 per cent of all the imports. Now that the islands have been annexed it is estimated that at least 95 per cent of all the importations will come from the United States.

WASHINGTON, Sept. 13.—The president has decided that it will be impracticable for the troops at Montauk to take part in the projected parade in New York City. All reports agree that the men will not be able to stand the fatigue of the parade before the first of next month at the earliest. As the parade was to occur next Saturday this renders the participation of the Montauk troops impracticable and the parade must consequently, if held at all, be composed of the troops coming in from Porto Rico, not exceeding two thousand in number. Department Of State. Nicaraguan Canal Commission, Washington, Dec. 26th, 1898.

To the Honorable, the Secretary of State, Washington, D. C.:

Sir: We have the honor to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 18th instant, enclosing copy of resolution of the Senate of the 18th December, requesting a report of progress made by this commission investigating the question of the feasibility and cost of construction of the Nicaraguan canal. This commission has understood, by which it was constituted and approved June 4, 1897, to require that routes heretofore proposed, having any merit, are to be considered, new routes that may appear to have merit are to be developed, and the entire region of canal possibilities to be examined with sufficient thoroughness to enable a just and comprehensive comparison, of the various routes to-be and the most desirable one selected. In short, to enable this commission to make a complete and exhaustive report.

LABORS OF THE COMMISSION.

With this view the commission visited Nicaragua, personally examined the entire canal region from ocean to ocean and employed some seventy engineers with their laborers and helpers, for ten months, in carrying out careful surveys and observations.

The entire field work has been obtained.

The reduction of this field work together with the compilation and comparison of former surveys going back nearly fifty years, has been in progress for more than two months; The commission believes that the construction of a canal across Nicaragua is entirely feasible.

The estimates for two of the best known characteristic routes have been nearly completed. These routes are known as the Maritime Canal Company's route and the Lull route. The estimated cost is $124,600 and $123,600 respectively.

IMMENSE UNDERTAKING.

The assumed dimensions are considerably greater than ever before proposed, both in length of locks and in width, depth and radius of curvature of canal. These increased dimensions have been made necessary by the demands of modern commerce, size and draft of modern ships, etc. This has necessarily made corresponding increase in the estimated cost, and is in no way inconsistent with the estimates made from the former surveys which contemplated a canal of smaller dimensions.

A canal of smaller dimensions, just sufficient for present trade, is being estimated. Such a canal would cost considerably less than the estimate for a canal suitable for modern necessities, which is referred to above.

It is the opinion of this commission that of the two routes herewith estimated for the one called the Lull route is the more desirable, because it is easier of construction, presents no problems not well within good engineering precedents, and will be a safer and more reliable canal when completed. The commission believes that the dimensions of construction preferred are better than would undoubtedly call for an expense within time.

COST MAY BE REDUCED.

Both of the routes referred to above admit of variance, which may reduce the cost. These are now being considered by the commission.

The work necessary for an exhaustive discussion of and report upon the entire canal problem, is being pushed as rapidly as its great magnitude permits, and when completed, the report will be sent to Washington without delay.

We are, with great respect, your obedient servants,

E. WALKER, Rear Admiral, U. S. N., President of Commission.

LEWIS N. HAUPT, Civil Engineer, Member.

I concur with the other members of the commission in respect to feasibility of a canal, but I think in view of the increased size of the canal estimated, and the difficulties incident to work in tropical countries, that the estimate is lower than it should be by a twenty per cent.

PETER C. HAYS, Colonel Corps of Engineers.

diocese of Marquette, has completed
the compilation of the regulations
for the season of Lent, and copies Of
an episcopal circular letter were
forwarded to all the priests in the
various parishes of this diocese. The
regulations were read from the pull
pits last Sunday. The regulations
are very much the same as those of
last year, with the exception that
there is added a recommendation to
the faithful to abstain from all in
toxicating liquors during Lent.


Working people and their families
are permitted to use flesh meat once
a.day on all fast days except Ash
Wednesday. Fridays and the
Wednesday and Saturday of Holy
week, during Lent. All are recon-
mended to avoid all public amuse
ments and to assist at Lenten de-
votions, which are held on two
evenings of the week.

How the Members and Associates


Are Elected-The Institutions Big


Fund and the Good Works That


Are Done with 1t.


To become a Royal aoademician, or at
all events an associate, is the ambition
Of every young artist, for membership
in the academy means much more than
the mere right to put the letters R. A.
after ene's name and to exhibit pictures
in the fine galleries at Burlington House.
In the first place, an aoademician is an
esquire by right and not merely by
courtesy, and, further, he is entitled,
should he ever come on hard times, to
a substantial pension of between $3.50
and e4O0 year. If he dies leaving his
widow unprovided for, the academy al
lows her a liberal sum for her mainte-
nance.


The associates and the associates wild
ows are also entitled to pensions on d
somewhat smaller scale, so that there
are many reasons apart from the honor
and glory why the painter, sculptor or
architect should wish to become MEM
Der of the powerful and wealthy body.


When therefore young artist begins
to get on, when he has his pictures we'll
hung year after year, when they find
ready buyers and are talked about in
society, he takes the first step toward
election by suggesting to one Of the
academicians that he should put his
name down Gil tie list of candidates.
Once down his name stays on the list,
either until he dies or is elected or vol
UNFAIRLY removes it. and this explains
why one finds on the roll of candidates
the names of many artists once popular,
but long since forgotten by the public.


When a vacancy occurs among the
associates, printed copies Of this list on
blue foolseap paper are sent to all the
members, together with request that
they shall attend at the academy on a
certain evening, when an election will
take place. The elections themselves are
conducted in singular and somewhat
complex fashion peculiar to the academy
"a method which took the place about
90 years ago Of the rough and ready sys-
tenn formerly in vogue.


Both academicians and associates are
allowed to take part in the election, and
when the members are gathered together
each scores out with a pencil the name
Of the artist for whom he wishes to
vote and hands the paper so marked to
the secretary. These scorings out are
known as scratches" at the academy,
and the secretary, after examining all
the papers, duly announces how many
scratches" have been given to each
candidate.


The election is then advanced another
stage. The president, who, by virtue of
his Office, occupies the chair, directs
that the names of all those candidates
who have received more than four
scratches" shall be inscribed in chalk
upon the blackboard, while those to
whom only one, two or three votes have
been given have no further chance of
being elected.


The academioians and associates then
vote again for the candidates whose
names are on the board. The two lead
ing men in this contest are now selected
for final ballot, the winner in which
becomes an associate of the Royal acad-
emy.


The academicians are elected in pre-
oisely the same manner, except that the
associates are the candidates instead of
the outsiders. All this system of
scratches" and. "blackboards' seems
cumbrous and unnecessary, but it is
said towork extremely well in practice.


Sometimes, though very rarely, tie
occurs, and in this case the president,
or, in his absence, the academieian who
temporarily takes his place, has cast
ing vote When Mr.. Ernest Crofts, the
battle painter, was elected, he tied in
the final ballot with Mr.. jackson, the
architect, and to Mr.. Calderon (who in
the absence of the late Sir John Millais
occupied the ohair) fell the difficult
task of making the final selection.


The associates have no voice in the
election of a president, the power of
voting resting entirely with the acade-
micians. Sir John Millais, the late
president, was elected by the unani-
nous vote of the members. a fact which
must have been extremely gratifying to
that great artist But on some other oc-
casions the fight for the presidentship
has been very severe indeed.


The post is well worth struggle, for
it carries with it substantial remunera-
tion, besides great social and artistic
distinction. The late Sir Francis Chan
trey left e100. 600 to the academy, out
of the interest of which salary of some
$500 or e900 year is provided for the
president.


The academy is immensely wealthy.
The receipts from the annual exhibitions
average from 100000 to e25, 900, and
it is believed that the money invested
in the hands of the trustees does not fall
far short of e500, 900. Out of this mon
ey the schools (in.which 200 or 800 stu
dents are instructed gratuitously) are
supported and great many pensions
and donations to deoayed artists are
given. Little is heard of these charities
by the public, but they are very consid-
srable, and the declining years of many
Did painters and sculptors are made easi-
sr by them.


Upon the academy also falls the ex-
pense of the annual banquet which
costs perhaps e4o0 or $500, besides any
number of minor charges, as, for exam
pie, the payment of the selecting and
hanging committees at the spring ex-
hibition. Pearson Weekly.

and $400 a year. If he dies leaving his
widow unprovided for, the academy al-
lows her a liberal sum for her mainte-
nance.


The associates and the associates' wives
are also entitled to pensions on a
somewhat smaller scale, so that there
are many reasons apart from the honor
and glory why the painter, sculptor or
architect should wish to become a mem-
ber of the powerful and wealthy body.


When therefore a young artist begins
to get on, when he has his pictures well
hung year after year, when they find
ready buyers and are talked about in
society, he takes the first step toward
election by suggesting to one of the
academicians that he should put his
name down on the list of candidates.
Once down his name stays on the list,
either until he dies or is elected or vol-
untarily removes it, and this explains
why one finds on the roll of candidates
the names of many artists once popular,
but long since forgotten by the public.


When a vacancy occurs among the
associates, printed copies of this list on
blue foolscap paper are sent to all the
members, together with request that
they shall attend at the academy on a
certain evening, when an election will
take place. The elections themselves are
conducted in singular and somewhat
complex fashion peculiar to the academy
—a method which took the place about
90 years ago of the rough and ready sys-
tem formerly in vogue.


Both academicians and associates are
allowed to take part in the election, and
when the members are gathered together
each scores out with a pencil the name
of the artist for whom he wishes to
vote and hands the paper so marked to
the secretary. These scorings out are
known as "scratches" at the academy,
and the secretary, after examining all
the papers, duly announces how many
"scratches" have been given to each
candidate.


The election is then advanced another
stage. The president, who, by virtue of
his office, occupies the chair, directs
that the names of all those candidates
who have received more than four
"scratches" shall be inscribed in chalk
upon the blackboard, while those to
whom only one, two or three votes have
been given have no further chance of
being elected.


The academicians and associates then
vote again for the candidates whose
names are on the board. The two lead-
ing men in this contest are now selected
for final ballot, the winner in which
becomes an associate of the Royal acad-
emy.


The academicians are elected in pre-
cisely the same manner, except that the
associates are the candidates instead of
the outsiders. All this system of
"scratches" and "blackboards" seems
cumbrous and unnecessary, but it is
said to work extremely well in practice.


Sometimes, though very rarely, a tie
occurs, and in this case the president,
or, in his absence, the academician who
temporarily takes his place, has the
casting vote. When Mr. Ernest Crofts, the
battle painter, was elected, he tied in
the final ballot with Mr. Jackson, the
architect, and to Mr. Calderon (who in
the absence of the late Sir John Millais
occupied the chair) fell the difficult
task of making the final selection.


The associates have no voice in the
election of a president, the power of
voting resting entirely with the acade-
micians. Sir John Millais, the late
president, was elected by the unani-
mous vote of the members, a fact which
must have been extremely gratifying to
that great artist. But on some other oc-
casions the fight for the presidency
has been very severe indeed.


The post is well worth struggle, for
it carries with it substantial remunera-
tion, besides great social and artistic
distinction. The late Sir Francis Chant-
rey left £10,600 to the academy, out
of the interest of which salary of some
$500 or $900 a year is provided for the
president.


The academy is immensely wealthy.
The receipts from the annual exhibitions
average from £10,000 to £25,900, and
it is believed that the money invested
in the hands of the trustees does not fall
far short of £500,900. Out of this mon-
ey the schools (in which 200 or 800 stu-
dents are instructed gratuitously) are
supported and great many pensions
and donations to decayed artists are
given. Little is heard of these charities
by the public, but they are very consid-
erable, and the declining years of many
old painters and sculptors are made easi-
er by them.


Upon the academy also falls the ex-
pense of the annual banquet which
costs perhaps £400 or $500, besides any
number of minor charges, as, for exam-
ple, the payment of the selecting and
hanging committees at the spring ex-
hibition. Pearson Weekly.

By the time the party reached the doors to the hotel, the crowd became so dense that progress was impossible. Colonel Bryan graciously responded to the cheers and calls for a speech, and, mounting a stone hitching block, said:

"I am glad to be with you again. I am greatly pleased that my regiment will have an opportunity of seeing the Confederate veterans and know that in our present struggle they will have an opportunity to fight with some of these old soldiers and their sons."

Colonel Bryan remained in Atlanta about two hours.

the jurisdiction of the supreme court; it is
not stated in that opinion. If the legislature

This is asserted, partly due to the moderation of President McKinley and the conservative manner in which the United States Minister General Stewart L. Woodford has dealt with the authorities in Madrid, and partly to the bitterness engendered by the alleged wanton attack of a band of insurgents upon the German sugar refinery in Cannanijo, in the Trinidad district of the Province of Santa Clara, Cuba, and the murder of four persons connected with the refinery, on March 15, which has taught Germany that Spain is unable to protect even the lives of foreigners in Cuba. As previously announced, the German Foreign Office is demanding immediate and full redress for this outrage and a German warship will soon be sent to Havana if satisfaction is not forthcoming in short order. The Spanish Ambassador here, Señor Mendez de Vigo, has had long conferences with Baron Von Bülow, the German Minister for Foreign Affairs, who conveyed to the Ambassador that Germany intended to have complete satisfaction, including an indemnity for the property destroyed and for the lives taken. The Ambassador also informed him that unless the redress was forthcoming, Germany would herself act, secure damages and punish the offenders. As incentive to quick preparation, Baron Von Bülow added that provisional orders had been cabled to the commander of the German warship Geier to sail in the direction of Cuba. The Spanish Ambassador promised he would exert himself to the utmost to comply with the German demands.

White in an interview said that while, thus far acting under instructions from Washington, he had not formally inquired of the German Government what its attitude would be in the event of war, he had nevertheless been repeatedly assured informally by Baron Von Bülow that Germany will in no case assume an unfriendly attitude toward the United States nor join in any possible combination of the Powers having that end in view.

The acquittal of Sheriff Martin for the
murder of strikers at Lattimer Pa. is a
simple triumph of justice. We are not
sorry that an indictment was brought
against him and that he was put on trial
for this alleged crime, although we have
believed from the first that he was only
acting in pursuance of his duty as the
chief peace officer of Luzerne county. It
is undoubtedly a hard thing for a man

arraigned for it as though he were a
criminal. Nevertheless the circumstances surrounding the event were such

presided gave wide latitude to the prosecution, and a great number of witnesses
were examined. All that can be known
about the shooting was made known by the
testimony of over a hundred witnesses.

a verdict of acquittal without hesitation,
and the sheriff is a free man.

is to Sheriff Martin, is far more important
in the influence it must have over all
peace officers. A sheriff in the simple
pursuit of duty, using the best judgment
he has, comes into collision with mobs
that will not obey his orders, and in
which men are killed and wounded, may
be convicted of murder; the effect would

course. No sheriff over whom the danger

pearance, and the crowd, after cheering

slowly dispersed.

Always cool, with most excellent water supply, superb bathing facilities, dry and level, there seems to be nothing in which it is lacking.

The health of the regiment continues to be very good. There are only three mild cases in the hospital.

Regimental Quartermaster Valentine has received from the government a supply of folding cots, invalids' chairs and folding chairs. These are intended for use in the field hospital. He has also for the officers of the regiment.

Flower Hospital.

John Taylor, an electrician of 225 East Twenty-eighth street, was taken to Flower Hospital three days ago to be treated for a broken leg and wrist. certain amount, the second week a sim-
ilar amount, and so on, week after
week. He writes without correction,
and never copies, producing just one
manuscript—the one which he sends to
the printer. Each week's work contin-
ues that of the preceding week. Though
the plan of the book is elaborated care-
fully in advance, this plan is not fol-
lowed strictly; from the "seething and
fermenting" in his head changes are
suggested to the author, and he makes
them. He has no secretary, amanuen-
sis, copyist, or assistant.

To write such books as he does with-
out copying or correcting, to create
works like the trilogy and "Quo Vadis"
by series of efforts, each one of which
gives a finished part, and each part be-
ing a seamless and flawless continua-
tion of the preceding, till the last, to-
gether with all the others, forms a com-
plete, unbroken whole, is perhaps the
most amazing tour de force in literary
experience. Sienkiewicz employs no
man or woman to help him. He makes
all literary researches himself; visits
and studies the places which he needs
to see; and when writing in Switzer-
land, Italy, France, or other countries,
takes with him all the books he re-
quires, and shuts himself in with them
during working hours, which for him
are from eight or nine till lunch at one
o'clock, and then a couple of hours later
on. He never writes after dinner in the
evening, and has so ordered his works
and days that he needs no assistance.

by the last Kansas legislature provid
ing for recording assignments of real
estate mortgages was yesterday de-
clared unconstitutional by Judge AL
den, of the district court in Kansas
City, Kan. The decision was in the
case of David H. Moore, a resident of
Ohio, against c. S. Mendenhan and
others. Mr. Moore has held mort
gage against certain Kansas City, Kan,

and Bridgens had bought the equity of
redemption in the property and they

closure under the recent act of the leg

cages executed and assigned prior to

ment of the same was recorded within

The Empire Club is by no means dead that is, according to latest reports from people who are in a position to know thing or two about the inside doings of fighting clubs. One man prominently connected with the turf has seemingly been a stumbling block to the interests of the club and its directors have finally concluded to dispense with the services of the gentleman, and they have accomplished it.

The Ryan and Choynski match is off and an attempt will now be made to match Choynski against McCoy, Maher or Sharkey. If the two former pugilists refuse to meet California Joe the club would not be shooting far off the mark if it matched Choynski against Sharkey, as the last time the local heavyweights met the contest did not terminate satisfactorily.

Sharkey is ready to fight any person and in any club. He should be given a chance when there is "a fair field and no favor," to demonstrate to the people of this city if he is really entitled to the distinction which he and his friends claim.

Any person who had seen Griffo against the Vallejo champion a few weeks ago and who witnessed the contest at the Olympic Club cannot but say that the Australian did not try to extend himself. Griffo must have had an object in reserving his speed and punches. Possibly he is playing for big game. At any rate McConnell was fortunate that Griffo held his left in check or his nose would have been discolored long before the decision was rendered. But with all due respect to McConnell it must be said that for a green one he is a surprisingly clever fellow, although a weak puncher.

George Bishop, better known as "Biddy," stated yesterday that he would like a turn at Jimmy Lawlor or any 125-pound fighter on the coast. Bishop is a promising looking fellow, who carries a pretty good record.

The Excelsior Athletic Club held a meeting on Tuesday evening, February 1, and the following officers were elected for the ensuing term: James H. Kennedy, president; John Horrigan, vice-president; Fred M. Waldstein, secretary; Gerald John Duffy, sergeant at arms; board of directors—Eugene Murray, Frank Skuse, Hugh McLaughlin, George Bastian and Henry Ahlers. The club is in good standing. It was decided to hold the next monthly exhibition on Monday evening, February 14. The main event will be an eight-round contest for valuable trophy between Jack Sullivan of the Jefferson Athletic Club and Jimmy Riley of the Excelsior Club.

It is but a little thing, yet on its proper use depends much of the happiness of modern man. Why civilized teeth should be so rotten is a question which has often been debated, and probably the true answer is more complex than some would think. Many good mothers are content to put all toothache down to lollypops, but that sugar in itself is not responsible for bad teeth is proved by the splendid "ivories" often possessed by negroes, who practically live upon the sugar cane and thrive upon it, too, during the whole of the season when it is in maturity. Dental decay is common enough, however, among negroes in towns, and it seems clear that the caries of the teeth which is so common among most civilized races is due not to any particular article of diet so much as to digestive and nutritive changes imposed upon us by our mode of life, and to some extent by the fact that by hook or crook we do somehow manage to live. Notwithstanding our bad teeth, whereas in a state of nature the toothless man soon dies.


Recognizing, then, that until the time arrives when some great social reformer either mends or ends our present social conditions, our teeth will tend to rot, and that, whatever the predisposing causes, the final act in the production of caries is the judgment of microbes on and around the teeth, we see that for long to come the toothbrush will be a necessity if health is to be maintained. It is only by the frequent use of this little instrument that those minute denominations can be removed which are at the root of so much mischief. A few elementary lessons in bacteriology would, we fancy, greatly startle many people and certainly would show them the futility of trusting to one scrub a day. The fact is that if people, instead of looking at the toothbrush from an aesthetic point of view and scrubbing away with tooth powders so to make their front teeth white, would regard it merely as an aid to cleanliness, they would see that the time to use it is after meals and at night, not just in the morning only when the debris left from the day before has been fermenting and brewing acid all night through. They would also see how inefficient an instrument the common toothbrush is unless it is used with considerable judgment. One of the secondary advantages of spending a good deal of money on dentistry is that at least one learns the value of one's teeth. By the time we have got them dotted over with gold stoppings and gold crowns we learn to take care of them, even although that may involve the trouble of cleaning them more than once a day and using perhaps more than one brush for the purpose.

cause to be indignant. Because a major
ity of its people are of Spanish descent
some sensation monger has started the
story that they are not loyal to the
United States. A baser slander on a
whole territory was never invented.
New Mexico has now been a part of the
United States for over half a century.
There has never been—except a small
riot at Taos in 1847—any kind of a re-
volt against the authority of the United
States. The mass of the people ac-
cepted American rule with rejoicing.
Both the rule of Spain and the subse-
quent rule of Mexico had been oppressive
and exacting, and the American troops
in 1846 were hailed as deliverers. The
generation of that day has passed away
and all Spanish-Americans in New Mex
ico—except perhaps some very aged
ones—have been born under the flag and
rejoice in being native-born American
citizens. They have neither love nor
sympathy for Spain, and their only re-
membrance of that monarchy is the des-
potic manner in which it once governed
the territory. Governor Otero is him
self one of this class, and his devotion to
the government of the United States
will be found typical of the entire Span
ish-American population of New Mex
ico.


THE starting of such rumor can only
be denounced in the most unmeasured
terms. If New Mexico is given the op-
portunity her people will furnish more
men in proportion to the population than
any state in the Union, and her volun-
teers will attest their loyalty on the
battlefield, to the confusion of those
who would circulate doubts concerning

They will issue circular letter explaining the purpose and inviting all the women of America to join, and copies will be sent to all prominent women's clubs and societies and to female colleges.

It is proposed to hold a mass meeting when affairs are in shape and appoint committee to wait on the local merchants dealing in French goods. Those ladies who have been purchasing French wines will also be asked to forego them and use only native wines, at least until the war is over. Mrs. Hobart, it is said, will become an active member. .-Philadelphia Record.

NORFOLK, VA, September 25.—(special.) One hundred and fifty men were put to work at the navy-yard to-day unloading the cargo of 1900 tons of coal from the collier Alexander, which vessel was to have sailed for New York to join the Iowa and Oregon. The Alexander commander noticed vapor arising from the hold of the vessel as she lay in Hampton Roads yesterday. He ordered the ship here, and Commodore Farquhar ordered the cargo taken out to-day. Near the bunkers is a large amount of oil. The Alexander is one of the colliers ordered to accompany the battleships to Manila. Information from the navy-yard is to the effect that the cargo of the Alexander is really afire. The more coal taken out the thicker is the smoke pouring from the hold. Every effort will be made to prevent the flames from reaching the oil.


That novel craft, the armed ferry-boat, Governor Russell of Massachusetts, went out on commission at the navy-yard to-day. Her crew, the Massachusetts naval reserves, were transferred to the receiving ship Franklin, to be mustered out of the service. The Russell was armed fore and aft with 5-inch guns, but the ordnance is being taken off. She had no occasion to use the guns on her stormy wartime voyage from Boston to Port Royal. The Russell will probably be returned to her owners at Boston.


The opening of trade between this port and Cuba was marked by the shipment to-day from the Lambert's Point piers of a cargo of coal to Santiago, on the schooner Hopkins.


It will require six months to complete the repairs to the great monitor Puritan, the champion heavyweight fighting machine of the world.


George Turner lies at his home near Portsmouth, almost at death's door, as a result of terrible injuries inflicted by unknown parties. Turner was found unconscious by a policeman; one cheek was almost entirely bare of skin, as was also his forehead, while his nose and mouth had been slit. There is no clue as to the identity of his fiendish assailant.


The Citizens Light Fuel and Power Company, which was chartered with heavy capital by the last Legislature, will have a hard time getting into the city, according to present indications. The City Gas Company, owning a half million dollar plant here, is fighting the admission of the new concern before the Council's committee. The contest will be long and fierce.


The campaign has started in earnest in this congressional district. The Wise Republicans opened headquarters to-day in this city, and the Democratic Committee follows suit tomorrow.

After using jury to decide in difference of opinion between neighbours, it is to be hoped some conclusion will be reached before the present trial is over. Ellis to pay for using the wharf. The first jury which heard the evidence could not agree.

Nansemond County Court launched into the case again to-day. There was some new legal talent in the case this time. Attorney J. R. McLemore, who has assisted with him Judge H. D. Tuck, of Norfolk; Judge L. H. Hawkes, of Suffolk, and Colonel W. Y. Griffin of Portsmouth, represent the plaintiff.

ELOQUENT PREACHER GONE

One of the best loved preachers Suffolk has known is dead, Richmond. The Rev. Dr. George C. Nandeslice breathed his last at six o'clock Thu. evening, after being unconscious more than a day. The end was peaceful. Dr. Nandeslice had been suffering for two or three weeks.

The deceased leaves seven children: Mrs. Lee Britt, of Suffolk; Dr. George Nandeslice, of Hampton; Mrs. Granny Nandeslice of Richmond; Attorney S. P. Nandeslice, and Misses May, Kate and Grace Nandeslice, Richmond.

Dr. Nandeslice was a former pastor of the Main Street Church in Richmond, and was well known. He was 72 years old.

In pursuance of his express wish, the remains will be inhum. in Suffolk for interment Saturday morning. The funeral will be conducted in Richmond.

MIGHTY STEAM HORSES

The two largest locomotive engines which ever passed through Suffolk will cross the Norfolk and Western track for the first time to-morrow morning. They are just from the factory. A pair of mighty steam horses will arrive mere over the Southern railway tracks, and be transshipped to the Norfolk and Western in East Suffolk. and details that were to be entered in

side of matters his difficulties appeared
overwhelming and his voice faltered.


For all the calm of her appearance,

with the dull light of London made
still duller by the fact that, out of re-
spect to the dead lying upstairs,
the blinds were down, he knew that
there were depths of feeling that he
dared not stir. Although he told her
of his power to supply her with mon-

stranger, he dared not offer her a grain
of that sympathy and affection for
which she craved.

repeated, vaguely, as if she could hard-

any trouble now that I am left to face it
all alone?"

liferous words at command—"I mean
with regard to the necessary expenses
incident to what has occurred."


The girl appeared unable to com-
prehend him.


"Many things have occurred that
money has no power to help," she said.

sympathize with you in the sad event.
Ah, poor brother!"


She turned quickly round, and ex-
claimed:

great sob, which she had with diff-

heard. "I've had so little, what with

me to act for you."

"The Jolly Musketeer," which is said to be a clever and amusing piece of work, will have its New York production at the Broadway Theatre tomorrow night. It is an operetta, with music by Julian Edwards and book by Stanislaus Stance, and it is the wagon which this year is hitched up to Jefferson De Angeli as a star. The story is of that favourite theatrical period, the time of Richelieu. The objection of that statesman and prelate to duelling has been emphasized on the local stage within the memory of living theatre-goers, and in "The Jolly Musketeer" it appears again. The King of the Cardinals makes some law against the duel; in this case Francois, Marquis de Chantilly, who has been condemned to death for the crime, but as a special favor on the part of the cardinal is to be allowed to take his own life. A short remnant of life may now and then be turned to a use to which one might not care to devote a whole life, and the Marquis determines to devote the fragment of his to aiding his friend Henri, Count De Beaupre, the jolly musketeer of the title. Die Compilation der Illinois Staatszeitung in den letzten Jahren bei American Germanen groß aufmerksam gepflegt und namhaft die von denselben veraltete Herausgabe deutscher als älterer mit Hinweisen und Glossen auf das Hochdeutsche beiprochen. Es ist dieser eine derartige Ausgabe erhielten, deren Anmerkungen aber nicht nur vor, sondern auch als werden. nämlich die des Professor Wilhelm Sell von Dr. B. B. Scherer, DOCTOR der Philologie und Professor der deutschen Sprache und Literatur an der Universität von Toronto bei der Macmillan Company in New York, 1898; sie entspricht dem von ihm verhandelten Literaturtextes selbst, wie es in den den der Illinois Staatszeitung erschienenen Ausarbeitungen klassischer deutscher Dichter der SAT-IT.


Prof. Scherer ist einer der besten Sprach- und Literatur-Kritiker in Amerika. Seine literarische Kritik ist weit, seine Philologie gefahren umgehend. Die vorige seiner literarischen Arbeit hat er seinerzeit im "Independent" auf Grund seiner trefflichen Ausgabe von Shakespeares richtiger Zeit zu lesen berichtet. Aus seiner Neuausgabe entgeht dem Leser viel, aber es ist die Pflicht des Kritikers, auch einmal auf der negativen Seite länger zu verweilen und die Tatsachen zu legen, im mehr, als dieser Band der Klassiker aus der ersten einer Serie III, die unter der Organisation des ausgezeichneten Germanisten und Defenders Landforscher M. Die Hauptlage, die man gegen das kurzfristige Urteil über Shakespeares Werke haben muß, ist die der Übereilung. Die Compilation alles dessen, was ohne rechtige Begabung des Merks irgendwo gefunden werden könnte, die Grundsicherheit der Bibliographie und die Berücksichtigung der Lage des Stoffes über den hat die Nichtachtung des Grundlegenden mit ihm gebrannt: "Von der Bezeichnetung zeigt über den Neuzustand."


Prof. Scherer erklärt in der Vorrede, seine Ausgabe sowohl für höhere Bildung (high schools) als auch des ersten Jahres in Colleges als Zeitgenossen dienen, aber da findet sich das Element warte mit den Daten; während er den unrettesten Schiller im Auge hat, versucht er zu gleicher Zeit den Literaturkenner, der die Literatur prüfen will zu untergehen. Nimmt er es gut in der Satz mit diesem Reiz. Die Folge aber ist: es fehlt an Einheit des Gales und Zweckes; man kann nicht zugleich zwei Herren dienen. New York, Oct. 10.—There is widespread fright in all the Republican camps throughout the country, according to the latest advices received in this city from leaders in all sections. They seem to be in that unenviable fix which leads every one to feel averse to listening to the woes that beset the party in other States inasmuch as all have troubles of their own.

This is particularly true of the congressional managers, who have learned from Chairman Babcock that all the energies of heaven and earth must be set at work to prevent the loss of the next House. Money is wanted everywhere. It is needed not only for the usual plans, but one important feature of the necessities that appear so formidable is that of arousing interest and enthusiasm and persuading Republican voters to surrender the apathy which has become so marked in the country districts as to be absolutely alarming.

Campaign meetings are not so well attended as heretofore even when there was no such indifference as seems to exist in Republican country circles as now, and campaign subscriptions everywhere are, to use the words of a disgusted leader who has recently visited the Roosevelt headquarters in this city, ridiculously nil.

The uneasiness of the Republican payers is increased by the confidence with which the Democrats are talking. On the other side the Democrats report advices showing "A greater amount of confidence in successes next month than has characterized their predictions for a long time."

Reports from ex-Congressman Kerr, secretary of the Democratic committee, are very encouraging. He does not believe that it will be possible for the Republicans to get out anything like the enormous vote they polled two years ago, especially in the East and the Middle West, and at the same time he is counting on the Democrats being able to hold their own much better in these localities as a result of the return to their ranks of many of the gold Democrats who voted the Republican ticket in 1896.

Mr. Kerr states his conviction that the Democrats will not lose a single district held by them in the present House, with the possible exception of one. He claims gains right straight through from New England west as far as Nebraska.

The Republicans are trying to keep their courage up about Illinois, but they seem almost certain to lose at least one of the Chicago districts—the Third—and there are some country districts, notably the Fifteenth, that they may lose.

Judge Van Wyck's little speech at the Manhattan Club gathering on Saturday night, in which he declared that the issues now are precisely the same as when Tilden led the Democracy to a magnificent victory in 1874, has met with a response that bodes no good to the machine ticket of Mr. Platt. Already there have been many telegrams and letters received from various parts of the State, showing a most favorable echo of his clear and modest utterances of the Democratic nominee. The Democrats of the State do not seem to have forgotten the glories under which the party made wonderful achievements under Tilden and Seymour, and from all appearances are impressed with the conviction that they are to be repeated under Van Wyck.

The local chapter of the Knights Of
Pythias celebrated the eighth anniver
sary of the founding of their chapter
Wednesday evening with social party
and dance, which proved to be one of
the most enjoyable parties ever given
by fraternal organization in Kenosha.
Among the Knights the anniversary
dance is always considered the social
event of the year, and the party last
evening was no exception to the rule.


The hall was very deliberately deco
rated for the occasion with plants and
pictures of the emblems of the order,
and the social committee did everything
in their power to see that all had a
splendid time, and in this they were
eminently successful. The party was
only for the Knights, but they were
privileged to bring with them their
sweethearts and wives to assist in
celebrating the event.


Cards and dancing were the features
of the evening, and all the ladies and
gentlemen entered into them with the
proper spirit. Excellent music was
furnished by Jacoby & Compton's
orchestra.


Supper was served at midnight,
after which dancing continued until
early morning.


The Teachers History Club.


The teachers History club held their
regular tortnightly meeting Wednes-
day evening at the home of Miss Belle
Stebbins on Park avenue. The even
ing proved very enjoy able one indeed,
the subject under consideration being
study of Greek Art and Architecture,
and its influence upon the national life
and the religion of the people.


The subject was a very interesting
one and for several hours the teachers
discussed the beauties of Grecian Art
and Architecture. The beauties of the
Ionic and the Doric furnished a good
ground for difference of opinion, and
several interesting discussions were
held. The program included paper
on Greek Temples, by Miss Anna

Riley, in which the writer brought out
in a charming manner the general
features of the Grecian architecture
which have made it world famous.


Miss Lance talked of the temples of
Greece, reading stories of artistic
beauty from such buildings as the
Pantheon and other Grecian temples.
The next paper was by Miss Eva j.
Riley, who took up the subject of art
in itself and discussed the Greek
Architectural sculpture.


This was followed by a very careful
ly prepared paper by Miss Frank
Stewart, on the types of the fourth and
fifth century sculpture. After the
reading of the papers Mr.. Marlowe led
general discussion on the relation
between the Greek art and religion.


The club has proved a great success,
and it's enthusiastic reception by the
teachers promises to make it great
assistance in the studies of historical
data.

tering or doing business in the city would

and more pronounced than the
shamefaced sentiment of like mean
ness that is whispered in some snob-
bish American circles. (2) That
the school rate seems to be the
most begrudged of English taxes,
the most sharply criticised, the
most grumbled at, and this to de-
gree for which there seems nothing
comparable in America. (3) That
the opposition to secular schools.
fostered by the church and ostensi-
bly, actuated by a desire for reli-
gious instruction in the schools, is
largely supported in reality by the
two sentiments indicated above.
~ y Looking, therefore, to the in
creasingly democratic conditions
that are inevitable in England, the
reluctance and factiousness of dis
position that appear among it's citi-
zens touching the vital matter of
popular education are ominous of
evil to the nation, and gravely lessen
its chance of holding, under the
reign of democracy, che high place
to which it rose under an aristo-
cratic regime.

The claim made that there is an overproduction of silver since 1873 as compared with gold, and that this is the cause of its fall in price, is absolutely without foundation. According to the tables issued by the Treasury Department August 16, 1893, showing the total production of gold and silver in the world at coinage value, it appears that from the year 1792, when our monetary system was founded, to the year 1852, being a period of 60 years, the total production of silver in the world, rating it at coinage value, was $1,769,197,000, and the total production of gold during that time was $960,236,000; that is, there was almost twice as much silver produced as gold. The production of each metal of course varied greatly during the different years, and yet the market ratio between the two metals remained practically the same during all that time. The tables show that during those 60 years there was variance of only seven-tenths of one point, or just about the cost of exchange. The same tables show that from 1852 to 1873 the total gold production of the world was $2,516,575,000, while the total silver production was $99,225,000; that is, there was 25 times as much gold produced as silver, yet the market ratio remained undisturbed during those 21 years, just as it had during the period of 60 years, when there was twice as much silver as gold. Again, the same treasury tables show that from 1873 to 1892, inclusive, the total gold production of the world was $2,176,505,000, while the silver production was $2,347,900; that is, the production of gold was nearly equal to that of silver. During the first two periods silver was money metal; during the last period it was not. The fact that during the first two periods, covering over 80 years, the market ratio remained the same, although the production of each metal varied greatly from time to time, shows that the market price or ratio was practically the same as the legal ratio or mint price, so long as both metals were used as money. Now, inasmuch as silver did not fall in value as measured in gold during 60 years in which there was twice as much silver produced as gold, it is clear that had silver not been demonetized it would not have fallen when the gold production was nearly equal to that of silver, as it was after 1873. Again, silver has not fallen in comparison with other property. By taking the average price of all commodities known to the markets it is found that a pound of silver will buy as great an amount of commodities, as great an amount of property, as ever. It is gold that has gone up. The law, by striking down the competition, has given gold monopoly. Practically, the gold dollar is a 200-cent dollar. JOHN P. ALTGELD

liner Paris arrived from Southampton

completed, equipped and in operation

reached here from Casas Grande, Mexico,
of the terrible fate which had befallen
the members of Black Jack's gang, who
escaped from this country several months

slain, and sought refuge from pursuit by
American officers in the fastnesses of the
Sierra Madre mountains of Mexico.

The Black Jack gang of desperadoes and
enthusiasts for several years terrorized
the entire border between here and the
Gulf of California, and it remained for
the avenging angels of the Mormon colo-
ny, to hunt down and annihilate the
gang.

On February 7, Mrs. S. Y. McDonald, a
Mormon woman, wife of prominent resi-
dent of one of the settlements, was
attacked by two unknown men. She was a
store keeper at Hound Valley, 50 miles
east of Casas Grande in an isolated lo-
cality. The ruffians split her head open
with hatchets, looted the store and es-
caped.

The brutal crime aroused the entire
Mormon community and the avenging an-
gels of the Mormon church were author-
ized to hunt down the murderers. They
searched the mountains in all directions.
On Sunday, March 6, the rendezvous of

plored region, 100 miles from Casas

ers closed in upon the outlaws, nine in

warning them that resistance meant

spiteful, well organized and successful
band of villains that has operated in the

wards were offered by the government
and the express companies for the cap-
ture of the outlaws if they were alive.

Mr. Atkinson, Representative Fourth District.

From the most casual perusal of this statute it will be seen that it is the plain duty of the Magistrate TO hear the complaining witness: the law says "he shall examine" him. The issuance of warrant in any case is a judicial function which neither the framers of our Constitution nor our Legislators ever contemplated should be exercised by the Executive, and the right to supervise the issuance of warrants claimed by the Attorney General's Department, is not only contrary to the spirit and genius of our Institutions, but is also clearly beyond the confines of, at least, the spirit, if not the letter, of our written law which I have above quoted. I may, in general terms, say that all of our laws in regard to the issuance of process of arrest and in matters of criminal procedure generally, have been derived by us from the English common law, which to obtain, the people of England, in the earlier history of that country, fought for inch by inch. Blackstone wrote his Commentaries on the Laws of England 1913 years ago. archy.

to Washington before leaving the country.

steamer Mariposa. conveying the Hawaiian
commissioners and 154 men of the 1st New
York Volunteers to Honolulu, sailed shortly
after O'Clock this morning. She was de-
tained at her dock all night awaiting the
arrival of delayed English mails.


The Examiner says:


when the Hawaiian commission embark
ed on the steamer Mariposa they found the
passenger deck stacked with boxes Of
onions. Senators Morgan and Cullom and
Representative Hit made a strong protest
to Captain Hayward against the ship
sailing in such condition. They de-
clared that it was an outrage and an
insult to the government to convert the
vessel which was to carry the official rep
resentatives on such an important mission
into freight ship. Further than this, they
asserted that it was unsafe to proceed to
sea under such conditions. Every berth on
the steamer was taken, and a number of
passengers could not get sleeping accommo-
dations. The commission was obliged to re-
main on the vessel, for the reason that it
could not secure any other means of trans
portation.'

CHEYENNE, Wyo., Dec. 5.—(Special.)—J. S. Palmer, director of the weather bureau at this place, has issued a review of the crop results in Wyoming during the year of 1898, which is in part as follows:

The months from January to April, inclusive, showed a marked deficiency in precipitation of moisture throughout the state. The average precipitation for the period was but 2.73 inches, while the normal should be 4.26. On account of the deficiency in moisture but little farm work was done until May, during which month there was an excess of precipitation, insuring an excellent crop of hay, but retarding the growth of grain. The weather during June was normal, being favorable to all crops. Hot, drying winds, and deficient rainfall marked July and August, droughty conditions prevailing at the close of July, relieved in part by generous rains early in August. A cold wave overspread the state early in September with killing frosts and freezing temperature. Grain had been harvested or was ready and little damage was done, excepting to vegetables. For the season the crop of hay, alfalfa, timothy and native grass, was unusually good throughout the state, both in quality and quantity. The early frosts of September damaged the cornfields and prevented a mature crop. On the whole the season has been a very favorable one for the farmers and ranchmen of the state. The ranges are in excellent condition for the present winter's grazing, and hay is plentiful so that little loss of stock is anticipated during the winter.

This committee feels confident Of its ability TO show that It is no fault Of ours that the National Committee Is not present as to-day, but It does not choose TO waste valuable time in wrangling over questions of official etiquette. We avow to be our sincere purpose now, as ever heretofore, to promote in every honorable way the reform movement on true Populist lines, and we deem the issues of the moment so momentous and the dangers threatening free government too imminent TO allow US TO pause TO consider personal grievances or affronts, or to permit wounded dignity to offend its duty.

Under present conditions, our beloved organization Is slowly, but surely, disintegrating, and our comrades are clamoring for aggressive action. Having in vain importuned those who assumed to be our superiors TO permit us TO aid them in the grand work OF reorganizing the People's party, that It may accomplish its glorious mission, we now appeal TO the people, the true source Of all political power."

The Referendum Committee appointed as follows: Messrs. Dixon, Of Missouri; Tracey, Of Texas; Reynolds, Of Illinois; Matsinger, of Indiana, and McGregor, Of Georgia.

A number Of rules were adopted For the government of the party, among them a rule that the National Organization Committee shall submit to vote Of the people's party any proposition when petitioned to do so by not less than 1,900 members Of the party.

On the adjournment of the Organization Committee of the People's party, the members OF the National Committee present met at the Laclede Hotel, and adopted the following resolutions:
"Resolved, That We, the members of the National Committee present, endorse the action taken by the ORGANIZATION Committee, and recommend that its provisions be carried into effect, believing that such action will harmonize all differences in the party."

There were seventy-four members OF the committee represented by members present or by proxies and letters, who favored a joint meeting OF the National Committee and Organization Committee in the spring.

Forty States were represented in the attendance at this meeting.

FIRST REFERENDUM VOTE.
ST. LOUIS, MO., January 1.—The Populists concluded their work in the city to-day by giving out the details of setting in motion their novel plan of taking a referendum vote Of the rank and file of their party. The question submitted is as follows:

"What date is your choice for holding a national convention for the nomination Of presidential candidates—Monday, July 4, 1898; Friday, May 26, 1899; or Thursday, February 7, 1900?"

The ballots are similar to the Austrian ticket, and will be polled by the local committees and Populist press. Milton Park, Of Texas, chairman of the National Organization Committee, and George W. Washburn, Of Massachusetts, member of the National Executive Committee, were among the last TO leave the city. Both men are highly pleased with the prospect Of unification of their party, and the prospective settlement Of the clamor for a new party.

A majority Of the National Committees have expressed themselves in favor Of an early conference for adjusting their difficulties and outlining a policy for the leaders Of the Middle-of-the-Road.

The element expressed themselves to-day as desirous that the work Of REORGANIZATION be conducted strictly within the party so as to merit the approval Of the National Committee.

ALEXANDRIA, Jan. 7, 1898


To His Excellency J. Hoge Tylor, Governor of Virginia:


Your letter to Mr. Leonard Narberth of this city, was shown me YESTERDAY. I desire to thank you for the kindness in which you speak of me and to assure you that I do not in the slightest way feel unkindly to you for not returning me to the Western State Hospital Board. It is perfectly natural that you should select some friend, as you have done. I have known Mr. Thornton for some years and you could not have made better selection.


The effort of myself and friends has been simply to place myself properly before you, having been informed that my position as party man and friend of yours had been misrepresented to you by Mr. L. C. Barley, the delegate from this city, and his friend or friends who called on you to urge my removal from the board. Now as to Mr. Barley I desire to say simply this: On the death of Judge Chichester, of Fairfax, a short while ago, Mr. Barley applied to Governor O'Ferrall to be appointed to that position. Gov. O'Ferrall wisely did not make this appointment but appointed a resident of Fairfax county, a most excellent gentleman, J. N. Lloyd. Mr. Barley's friends thinking it best for their interests that he should be on the bench in Alexandria and Fairfax counties induced him to announce himself for the legislature and then to offer himself as a candidate for the judgeship. To give legality to this Mr. Barley removed—a fact known to very few—his legal residence to the county of Alexandria, a mile or two from the corporation line. Mr. Barley offered himself as candidate for the Legislature from Alexandria county, and no one else being string to go into scramble for the position, Mr. Barley was selected without opposition. It has been said by very many here, and am perfectly convinced of it, that Mr. Barley ran for the Legislature for the express purpose of having himself elected judge of the counties of Fairfax and Alexandria, in neither of which he ever absolutely resided for a moment. Mr. Barley, in an interview published in a Washington paper, says he did not go out of the city of Alexandria "as Mr. Beckham did," to ask an appointment. I suppose he must allude to this judgeship. I have never asked a member of the Legislature to vote against Mr. Barley or to vote for Judge Love! I did state, perfectly honestly, in an interview with Mr. Geo. X. Pickett that I did not consider Mr. Barley a citizen of Alexandria county, and I do not know a citizen of this city who does. I say now, and have always felt, that a man to be selected a judge to sit on cases affecting the life and property of other people ought to be one thoroughly conversed in law and who has proved himself capable of taking care of his own affairs. What prominence in legal matters has Mr. Barley attained that would entitle him to be selected a judge? Who, save one, with an immense amount of cheek, would ask to be appointed judge over the people in whose county he did not reside? I have never spoken unkindly of Mr. Barley, and some people here know I have gone to his rescue when he needed a friend. Dr. Smith is my family physician and personal friend. I had never heard until yesterday that his name had been mentioned as a member of the hospital board. My duties there were not in the line of physician. I attended to the business management and left other matters to the staff of the hospital. I have nothing to regret as to my connection with the hospital and have done my duty to the State, and if Mr. Barley thinks he has done what is best for the people of my district, it is all right. I think he will find very few in Alexandria to agree with him. I am, with great respect, very truly yours,

CHICAGO, ILL, Dec. 10, 1898 EDITOR
HERALD, Columbia, Tenn.— The statement has been made to me that not one in ten of our voting population knows, understanding, what bimetallism is, and I have been asked to define it.

It is the right to use either of two metals for money—gold and silver. The supply reaches the people through the mints of the government, by the mints being open to coin all that comes. The option, known as the bimetallic option, is with the government and the people to use either of the two metals in the discharge of their obligations. If the government is paying its soldiers, its employees, its numerous officials or other obligations, under bimetallism, it has the right to pay in money made from either metal. If the people are paying their taxes to the city, state or nation, or purchasing postage stamps, or discharging their obligations to each other, under bimetallism, they have the right to pay in money made from either of the two metals.

It thus places the two metals in competition with each other to supply the demand for money. Thus one relieves the strain upon the other—as one eye relieves the strain upon the other.

With the option with the people to use money made from either of the two metals they controlled the demand and placed that demand on the one that was the most accessible. If silver grew cheaper they shifted the demand to it and took the demand away from gold; hence silver rose in commercial value and gold declined. If gold came to be the cheaper they, the people, used it, thus shifting the demand to gold and taking it away from silver. And it was the demand thus controlled by the people, as such and as government, that practically maintained the commercial parity of the two metals for all time prior to 1873.

Following the act of 1873 the option was given to the creditor to demand either of the two metals—just the reverse of bimetallism, and the result is that the creditor demands the dearer of the two metals—and the dearer it gets the more apt he is to demand it. Under bimetallism, the use of two metals, the people could be depended upon, naturally, to shift the demand automatically to the cheaper of the two metals when either was cheaper than the other. Taking the demand away from the dearer brought it down in value, and placing it on the cheaper brought the latter up in value—thus the commercial value of the two was maintained at parity. The effect was to give practically the volume of the two metals to our stock of metallic currency; and furnished the basis for an equally enlarged volume of paper money under a redemption monetary system.

The theory of the open mints to coin all that came of either metal was to let the supply reach the people. Close the mints to either and you shut off the supply and force the use of the other. The open mints to the two metals gave the supply and the people controlled the demand. If silver rose in value it stunned the mints and was shipped abroad to pay debts—as it was for a time prior to 1873—or in exchange for gold, and the latter was added to the domestic supply that went to the mints and vice-versa. Neither could rise in value and extort tribute from the people so long as the other was in competition with it—Open mints and option with the people.

The government bought neither metal. The mints were open to coin all that came of either metal, and to give back the coins to those who brought the bullion. It was coined free because it was statesmanship for the government to facilitate and provide way for money, one of the principal functions of society. Bimetallism therefore consists of open mints and option with the people to use either. Under bimetallism there is no such thing as gold contracts, it is "coin" contracts.

The reason why the demand, shifted from one metal to the other exerted by a nation like the United States, will maintain the commercial parity of the two metals, is because of the world limited supply of the two metals. All the gold in the world, at the present time, available for money, will go in the cube of — feet; all the silver in the cube of — feet. All the gold in the United States will go in an average size bedroom; all the silver in almost any farmer's barn. W. W. HARVEY.

It was midnight on North Clark street and a carriage was just rolling out of livery stable. The fashionable but somewhat unsteady gentleman in the carriage leaned out of the window, produced a roll of bills and asked what his ride would cost him. The liveryman, evidently an old friend, and as unsteady on his feet as the other, waved his hand:

"Not a cent? Not a cent! It's on me!"

The man in the carriage looked afraid.

The man in the carriage climbed halfway out.

"I guess I can pay for any rides I get," he bellowed, waving his roll again.

"You've got to take it!"

"You can't make me take it!"

"I say I will!" and the man in the carriage came out entirely.

"This is your money. I pay for any rides I get."

"The great secret of success IN road
making and bookkeeping is to drain
the roads. and keep the roads drained
by keeping the bitches open," writes
John Gilmer Speed, on Chow to have
Good Country Roads," in the August
Ladies' Home Journal. "Ihe old
method was to run plow through
the side bitches and throw the dis
turbed soil, sod and all, in the middle
of the road. There it would stay till
a heavy rain came to wash this soil
back into the bitches and fill them up
again. If there were money enough
this kind of thing would be done over
and over again, as often as four times
in q year. Where there were wet
spots, broken stone or gravel would be
placed in the road and left for the
passing wagons to wear this metal into
ruts. The money spent was absolute
ly thrown away.


"By the new process all the road
mender needs to do is to provide
bitches and outlets for them, and then
so shape the road that the water fall
ing in a rainstorm will run off at once
into the bitches. The water must not
be suffered to run in the road, but off
the road. The rainfall, being thus
simply and effectively disposed of, be-
comes most beneficial instead of
destructive agent; it cleans and shapes
and hardens the roadway, instead of
washing it away and deepening the
ruts. When there are wet places,
such as springs, in the roadway, gravel
and broken stone will not cure such
things. The water must be drained
off underneath the roadway and into
the bitches by means of pipe or blind
drains. The whole thing is so simple
that any one can easily master the
principles and put the details into
practical operation"

all classes of workers. The nurses receive
instruction, both theoretical and practical,
quite like that given in the best training

and meeting with most gratifying success.

WASHINGTON, D. C., July 17.—
Incident with the occupation of Santiago: there are a vast variety of questions which are being considered by the President and his cabinet respecting the future political conditions which are to obtain there. There will have to be settled whether the government of Santiago province shall be military one or civil one with military powers vested in the executive officer, or other form of administration.


Unlike the Philippines, which, although nominally in our possession, are not formally so, all questions of jurisdiction over and administration of the occupied territory of Santiago must be met immediately. Among the questions asked in relation to the difficulties of the Indian frontier war is the reason why the difficulty of obtaining water blocks our advance but does not hamper the enemy. The answer is that our troops had in one camp upward of 25,000 baggage animals. There were oxen, mules, donkeys, and camels. The former are all very thirsty creatures, and even the camels are credited with vastly larger powers of sustaining thirst than they possess. Maj. H. G. Leonard, after 11 years experience as a transport officer, is convinced that camels should, if possible, be watered every day, that they cannot be trained to do without water, and that, though they can retain gallons of water in the sacs of the stomach, four or five days' abstinence is as much as they can stand, in heat and with dry food, without permanent injury.


The record of the sufferings of the unfortunate animals which accompanied a ill-arranged expedition in the Eastern desert is a timely comment on this opinion. It is very doubtful whether the minority of the various desert animals willingly go without water, or, in fact, do so to any great extent. They drink sparingly, and can probably, by habit and practice, go for long periods without drinking, more than species living in well-watered districts. But the absence of any special provision for the internal storing of water, except in the camels and some tortoises, seems to indicate that this power of long abstinence is only an accident of nature. Nor is it often possible to be certain that stores of water do not exist in deserts; stores perfectly well known to the animals, though not to travellers. This is especially the case in rocky deserts such as the Rayuda desert and that between Suakin and Berber.

Washington, July 8.—Gen. Shafter reported all quiet yesterday in the camp before Santiago, and the best belief of the officials here is that the same state of affairs obtains to-day. The army is losing nothing by its rest, and according to the General's account, is gathering strength. More reinforcements are due to-day or to-morrow, and when they arrive it is expected that the assault on the city will be resumed. It is hoped this will be tomorrow, though so far as the army is concerned it will not advance before reinforcements arrive unless in order to repel an attack from the Spaniards. Gen. Shafter and Admiral Sampson had conference day before yesterday and as a result the fleet is going to make another try at the fortifications at the mouth of the harbor tomorrow. If the army is ready this will partake of the nature of a general attack; if not, then the navy's action will be simply in the line of execution of a policy of reducing Santiago by stages according to regular siege methods. While cooperating as far as possible with the army the navy is not to be sacrificed in this attack upon the Spanish forts.
